q-214215.problem:

$$

$$

{{field-3}}.
q-214215.worked_solution:
First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

Our relation is defined on $\{\alpha ,\beta ,\delta ,\gamma \},$ and has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true. Therefore, since for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)\in R & \,⟹\,(y,x)\in R, \\ (x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R & \,⟹\,x=y,\end{aligned}
$$

the relation is $\text{both symmetric and antisymmetric}.$

(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.

First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

Our relation is defined on $\{0,1,2\}.$ Notice that:

- $(-1,2)\in R$ and $(2,-1)\in R.$ So, the relation is $\text{not antisymmetric}.$

- $(0,2)\in R$ and $(2,0)\notin R.$ So, the relation is $\text{not symmetric}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the relation is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric.

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

Our relation is defined on $\{1,3,4,5\}.$ Notice that:

There are no other pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y$ in the relation. So, for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

q-214214.worked_solution:
First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

Our relation is defined on $\{♠,♡,♣,♢\},$ and has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true. Therefore, since for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)\in R & \,⟹\,(y,x)\in R, \\ (x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R & \,⟹\,x=y,\end{aligned}
$$

the relation is $\text{both symmetric and antisymmetric}.$

First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

We are given elements of the adjacency matrix in the following highlighted cells outside the diagonal:

|  | $-3$ | $2$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-3$ | $0$ |  | $0$ |
| $2$ | $0$ | $1$ |  |
| $7$ |  | $1$ | $0$ |

As a result, the relation contains the pair $(7,2).$ Since $R$ must be antisymmetric, we require 

$$
(2,7)\notin R.
$$

So, the cell corresponding to this element must be $0.$

|  | $-3$ | $2$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-3$ | $0$ |  | $0$ |
| $2$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $7$ |  | $1$ | $0$ |

We do not have enough information to determine whether $(-3,2)$ and $(7,-3)$ are the elements of $R.$
